entries.event: Treaty of Saginaw signed; Chippewa peoples retain fishing rights in exchange for land cession.
St. Louis, Michigan incorporated.
Oil discovered in the region.
Velsicol Chemical founded in Chicago by Joseph Regenstein.
Midwest Refinery opens in Alma on the Pine River.

Michigan Chemical incorporated for ethyl bromine and road-dust-control products; McClanahan Refinery opens; Saginaw City Council calls for Pine River protection; University of Michigan research documents water pollution.
Journal of Industrial Hygiene publishes a study warning of health dangers from compounds like DDT.
Leonard Refinery acquires the McClanahan property in Alma.
121 St. Louis citizens file contamination complaints against Michigan Chemical.
Michigan Chemical begins DDT production for military use against malaria.
DDT dangers publicized; magnesium oxide animal feed supplement production begins.
Publication warns of developing DDT resistance.
New York Times reports on growing DDT resistance; flame retardant production starts.
Paul Müller wins the Nobel Prize for the discovery of DDT.
MSU ornithologist George Wallace begins DDT studies.
Michigan DNR documents extensive DDT contamination; rare earth production and radioactive waste disposal commence.
Michigan DNR issues a negative report on the Pine River.
DDT production ends.
Wallace testifies before the U.S. House Subcommittee on Fisheries and Wildlife.
Rachel Carson completes Silent Spring; Velsicol threatens a lawsuit.
Velsicol owns 50.5% of Michigan Chemical.
Velsicol completes its purchase of Michigan Chemical.
Velsicol funds a publication attacking Carson's work.
Michigan DNR issues another negative report on the Pine River.
Chicago and North Western Railway acquires Northwest Industries.
PBB-based flame retardant production begins.
PBB accidentally shipped to Farm Bureau Services feed facility in Climax, Michigan.
PBB contamination discovered in farm animals; quarantine begins; Dr. Tom Corbett and Irving Selikoff start research.
Dr. Alpha Clark McBain confirms PBB is causing animal health problems.
Michigan PBB Registry established, tracking over 4,000 exposed people; Michigan sues Velsicol.
Thames Television releases the documentary The Poisoning of Michigan.
Velsicol closes the Michigan Chemical plant; CBS delays the Slaughter dramatization until after the elections.
Superfund (CERCLA) passed by Congress; Northwest Industries headquarters moves to Denver.
Bitter Harvest, a film about the PBB accident, opens.
Consent Judgment signed between Velsicol and federal/state officials.
The former plant site and Gratiot County Landfill become Superfund sites; Michigan DNR begins fish sampling.
Plant burial completed; Bill Farley buys Northwest Industries; Velsicol managers refuse to take possession of the contaminated sites.
ATSDR warns of fish contamination and human health exposures.
Former workers settle with Velsicol; EPA requests an Army Corps of Engineers river study.
Alma College publishes a policy-failure assessment.
ATSDR reports containment failures; river fish show unacceptable DDT levels.
Michigan DNR sampling reveals DDT levels have doubled since 1989.
State staff report on fish contamination in the impoundment.
EPA holds a public meeting announcing river problems.
Task Force formed; EPA begins emergency removal planning; Velsicol purchases $100 million in insurance.
Emergency removal action begins; Total Petroleum closes; Task Force seeks an NIEHS grant.
Task Force files a bankruptcy claim; obtains a $13 million supplemental environmental project.
Task Force files a second human health grant request; demands a CDC response.
University of Michigan Law School provides assistance; Fruit of the Loom settles for $42.5 million; NAPL migration verified.
Horse Creek remediation completed.
pCBSA found in St. Louis drinking water; Task Force compels ATSDR/CDC participation; wins claim against Oxford Automotive.
St. Louis sues to overturn the settlement.
EPA determines the 1982 containment system failed; Robert Bullard speaks on environmental justice.
DOJ sides with Fruit of the Loom; Eugene Kenaga DDT Conference hosted.
Pine River Statement on DDT published and discussed at the Stockholm Convention.
Velsicol Burn Pit returned to the Superfund National Priorities List.
St. Louis wins its water system lawsuit.
EPA finalizes the remediation Record of Decision; Emory University PBB team collaboration begins; residential soil cleanup starts.
Task Force hosts its first joint PBB health screenings with Emory University.
New water system operational through the Gratiot Water Authority; athletic field cleanup completed.
"Birds Falling from Sky" press articles appear; Intergenerational Risk Conference hosted; residential soil remediation completed.
Thermal treatment of plant site wastes begins; PBB Oral History Project funded.
EPA studies floodplain remediation; thermal treatment continues; DDT sampling at school fields shows high spots.
University of Michigan PFAS conference held; Phase II thermal treatment begins.
Plant site remediation expands; floodplain operable unit planned; burn pit remediation advances.
Conference commemorates the 50th anniversary of the PBB accident.
